title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 44
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Where the Sea Meets the Ledger
passages.text:
A. A port is not a place where ships stop but a place where the cost of changing transport mode is lowest. Moving goods between a vessel and a vehicle is expensive, slow and the point at which damage and theft occur, and every feature of a port's design and location follows from minimising that transfer rather than from anything nautical. Ports arise where the land route and the sea route can be joined cheaply.

B. Natural advantages mattered enormously until they could be bought. Deep water close to shore, shelter from prevailing weather, a river giving access inland and a firm shoreline for building were the conditions that made a harbour, and settlements grew where they coincided. Dredging, breakwaters and piling made it possible to manufacture those conditions, at a price, and the map of major ports has been redrawn accordingly.

C. The relationship between a port and its city was once close and has been severed. Loading and unloading by hand required enormous numbers of workers living within walking distance, and the warehouses, markets, brokers and shipping offices that clustered around them made the waterfront the commercial centre. That arrangement was destroyed within a couple of decades by mechanisation, and the resulting empty land is why so many cities have a redeveloped former dock.

D. Modern ports moved because ships grew. Larger vessels need deeper water, longer berths and vast flat areas for storage that no historic urban waterfront could supply, so operations relocated downstream or to entirely new sites, taking the employment with them. A port today may handle many times the tonnage of its predecessor with a small fraction of the workers, and be located where almost nobody lives.

E. The economics have concentrated traffic into fewer places than most people expect. A very large ship is cheap per container only if it is filled and turned around quickly, which requires the equipment and depth that only a few ports possess, so lines serve a small number of hub ports and distribute onwards by smaller vessels, rail and road. This makes the network efficient and gives individual ports considerable bargaining power over the regions behind them.

F. What a port now competes on is the land side rather than the sea side. Vessels can be handled quickly almost anywhere with the right cranes; what differs is whether containers can leave promptly by rail and road, whether customs clears them without delay, and whether the surrounding roads can absorb the traffic. Investment in the quay without investment in what lies behind it produces a port that unloads efficiently into a queue.

passages.title: Stronger Than It Should Be
passages.text:
Spider silk has been described as stronger than steel for so long that the claim has become an obstacle to understanding what is actually remarkable about it. Compared by weight, the best silks do rival steel in tensile strength, which is genuinely impressive for a material extruded at ambient temperature and pressure from a protein solution. Compared in absolute terms a steel cable is far stronger, and the more useful comparison is not strength at all.

What distinguishes silk is toughness, which is a different property from strength and more useful for the job silk does. Toughness is the energy a material absorbs before breaking, combining how much force it withstands with how far it stretches, and a web must absorb the energy of a flying insect without breaking or bouncing it back out. A material that is strong and brittle would fail at this; silk stretches substantially before it fails, and it is this combination that no manufactured fibre matches across the board.

A single spider produces several silks with different properties from different glands. The frame of a web is made from a stiff, strong silk; the capture spiral from a stretchy one coated in glue; the wrapping of prey and the protection of eggs use others again. Treating spider silk as one substance obscures the more interesting fact, which is that the animal manufactures a small range of engineered materials and selects between them according to the task.

The manufacturing process may be more valuable than the product. The silk protein is stored as a concentrated liquid and converted to a solid fibre by changes in acidity, salt concentration and mechanical shear as it passes through the duct — at body temperature, in water, with no solvent and no waste. Industrial fibre production of comparable performance requires high temperatures, petrochemical feedstocks and considerable energy, and understanding the spider's method has been a goal for decades because of the process rather than the material.

Attempts to produce it at scale have failed in an instructive way. Spiders cannot be farmed, because they are territorial and cannibalistic in density, so the approach has been to transfer the genes into organisms that can be grown — bacteria, yeast, plants, goats — and this reliably produces the protein. What it does not produce is the fibre: the protein must then be spun, and reproducing the duct's precise sequence of chemical and mechanical conditions has proved to be where the difficulty actually lies.

The lesson generalises beyond this one material. Biological materials achieve their properties through structure and processing rather than through exotic ingredients, and copying the composition without the manufacturing conditions produces something with the right chemistry and the wrong performance. The recurring finding in this field is that the recipe was never the secret.

passages.title: The Floor Under Wages
passages.text:
The minimum wage is the rare economic question where the textbook prediction and the accumulated evidence have diverged sharply enough to change the textbook. The simple model is clear: set a price floor above the market rate for labour and employers will buy less of it, so employment among the lowest-paid falls. This reasoning is sound within its assumptions, and its assumptions turn out not to describe low-wage labour markets well.

The empirical turn came from comparing places rather than modelling them. Studies contrasting employment in neighbouring jurisdictions where one raised its minimum and the other did not — similar economies, similar workers, different policy — repeatedly found employment effects close to zero, and the finding has survived several rounds of methodological dispute and considerable hostility. It is not universal, and it is not what the simple model predicted.

The most persuasive explanation is that employers of low-paid workers have more wage-setting power than the model assumes. Where workers face limited alternatives, costs to changing jobs, and imperfect information about what other employers pay, a firm can pay below what an additional worker is worth without losing everybody, and a mandated increase in such a market can raise wages without reducing employment — because the wage was below the competitive level to begin with.

Adjustment happens through channels the employment debate tends to ignore. Firms facing higher wage bills raise prices modestly, accept lower profits, reduce turnover costs because fewer workers leave, gain from workers who are better rested and better trained, and sometimes reduce hours or scheduling flexibility rather than headcount. Measuring only the number of jobs misses most of how the adjustment actually occurs.

The level is where the evidence genuinely stops. Findings of minimal employment effect come from increases within the range that has actually been tried, and they cannot be extrapolated to a floor set far above local median earnings; a minimum wage high relative to what a regional economy supports is a different proposition from one that is moderate. The honest position is that moderate increases have not produced the predicted losses and that no evidence establishes where the point of harm lies.

What is often lost is that the minimum wage is a poor instrument for the problem it is asked to solve. It raises the pay of low-paid workers, many of whom are not in low-income households, and does nothing for those with no work at all; earnings supplements and transfers reach poor households more precisely. The two are complements rather than substitutes, and treating either as the whole answer is what makes the argument so much more heated than the evidence warrants.
